title: Tokens and names: precise source with clear meaning
goal: Split a statement into parts and identify which names you may change.

prerequisites.text: You can read the main frame and an int declaration.

sections.title: From the task to an operation
paragraphs: In int itemCount = 3;, int is a keyword: the language reserves it for an integer type. itemCount is an identifier chosen by the author; 3 is a numeric literal; = supplies the initial value and ; ends the declaration. These meaningful pieces of text are tokens.

A name starts with a letter or an allowed underscore and may then contain digits. For our own names, use Latin letters without a leading underscore. itemCount and itemcount are different names: case matters. A space separates int from its name; no space belongs inside itemCount. Do not use reserved words as names.

sections.title: Split a statement into parts and identify which names you may change.
trace: Type, name and value have different roles.
Names in the expression must match their declarations.

sections.title: Change one condition and check the prediction
paragraphs: Rename itemCount to quantity in its declaration and expression.
The name changes, not the value 3.
Find both uses of the name; the compiler distinguishes case.

sections.title: When the result differs
paragraphs: Renaming only the declaration leaves an unknown name in the output expression: this is a build error, not a wrong price.

sections.title: Now solve your own task
paragraphs: Calculate 4 items at 15 using quantity and price. Explain which tokens are keywords and which you chose.
Practice contains a separate starter. Predict the result before changing your program. Returning to the example does not replace your source.

terms.definition: A meaningful lexical unit such as a name, literal, or operator; not necessarily one character or a word separated by spaces.
A name form used in declarations and references to program entities.
A word with a special grammatical role, such as int or return; it cannot be declared as an ordinary quantity name.
A value written directly in source, such as 250 or "duration_ms=".
A team agreement about readable names that may be stricter than the language syntax.
A consistent name change in a declaration and all corresponding uses while preserving meaning.
